title: Mitochondrial depolarization stabilizes the vitamin B12 chaperone MMADHC in the cytosol to increase MTR activity
abstract: Of the ~1100 mitochondrial proteins, only a handful like PINK1 and ATFS-1 are known to stabilize and relocalize upon collapse of the proton motive force (PMF) to execute signaling roles. To systematically identify genes that increase exclusively at the protein level upon PMF collapse, we performed a joint proteomic and RNA-seq screen. The screen revealed 10 candidates (six mitochondrial), including the vitamin B<sub>12</sub> chaperone MMADHC and cytosolic B<sub>12</sub>-dependent methionine synthase (MTR). MMADHC is short-lived across cell types and we show that its levels increase with PMF collapse. MMADHC stabilization precedes PINK1 activation in a time course of increasing mtDNA depletion, suggesting greater sensitivity to PMF collapse. MMADHC accumulates in mitochondria with LONP1 inhibition but in the cytosol upon PMF collapse, likely due to mitochondrial import failure. Cytosol-stabilized MMADHC increases MTR levels and activity. Altogether, the mitochondrial PMF regulates the cytosolic B<sub>12</sub>-dependent MTR, integral to one-carbon metabolism, by controlling the stability and compartmentalization of the B<sub>12</sub> chaperone MMADHC.

match.title: Mitochondrial depolarization stabilizes the vitamin B12 chaperone MMADHC in the cytosol to increase MTR activity
match.authorString: Rath SP, Li Z, Guha A, Dong F, Banerjee R, Mootha VK.
match.abstractText:
Of the ∼1100 mitochondrial proteins, only a handful like PINK1 and ATFS-1 are known to stabilize and relocalize upon collapse of the proton motive force (PMF) to execute signaling roles. To systematically identify genes that increase exclusively at the protein level upon PMF collapse, we performed a joint proteomic and RNA-seq screen. The screen revealed 10 candidates (six mitochondrial), including the vitamin B12 chaperone MMADHC and cytosolic B12-dependent methionine synthase (MTR). MMADHC is short-lived across cell types and we show that its levels increase with PMF collapse. MMADHC stabilization precedes PINK1 activation in a time course of increasing mtDNA depletion, suggesting greater sensitivity to PMF collapse. MMADHC accumulates in mitochondria with LONP1 inhibition but in the cytosol upon PMF collapse, likely due to mitochondrial import failure. Cytosol-stabilized MMADHC increases MTR levels and activity. Altogether, the mitochondrial PMF regulates the cytosolic B12-dependent MTR, integral to one-carbon metabolism, by controlling the stability and compartmentalization of the B12 chaperone MMADHC.

Significance Statement

Humans have only two vitamin B12-dependent enzymes – mitochondrial MMUT and cytosolic MTR – and both require a common B12 chaperone MMADHC. We discover that MMADHC is a low abundant, short-lived protein that is continuously imported and degraded by energized mitochondria. Upon collapse of the mitochondrial proton motive force, MMADHC accumulates in the cytosol and increases the levels and activity of MTR, critical for one-carbon metabolism. This PMF-dependent regulation of MMADHC stability and localization is important for understanding cofactor rationing and spatiotemporal compartmentalization of B12 metabolism.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This preprint presents an early but focused story about how mitochondrial depolarization can stabilize the vitamin B12 chaperone MMADHC in the cytosol, with the downstream effect of increasing MTR activity. The strongest available signal is not citation volume yet, but documented reuse: the record shows one biomedical article mention in Europe PMC. Broader public attention and citation uptake are still sparse in the current record, which is consistent with a very recent bioRxiv posting.

Full narrative

Rath, Li, Guha, Dong, Banerjee, and Mootha use a joint proteomic and RNA-seq screen to ask a targeted signaling question: which genes rise at the protein level when the mitochondrial proton motive force collapses, even if transcript levels do not? In that search, they identify MMADHC as a notable candidate, linking mitochondrial depolarization to the cytosolic stability of a vitamin B12 chaperone and to increased activity of MTR, a B12-dependent enzyme central to methionine metabolism. The abstract positions this work alongside a small set of known proteins such as PINK1 and ATFS-1 that are stabilized and relocalized during mitochondrial stress to perform signaling roles.

From an impact perspective, the record is still early. OpenAlex lists zero citations, and scite records no citation activity yet. That should be read as a timing signal rather than a judgment on significance: the work appeared in late 2025 as a bioRxiv preprint, so downstream scholarly uptake may simply not have had time to accumulate. Public discussion signals are likewise quiet in the available record.

What is visible today is a modest but concrete reuse signal. Europe PMC records one downstream biomedical article mention, indicating that the paper has already been noticed in scholarly literature tracking even before citation counts appear. The article is also indexed across multiple repository instances, including open versions, which should aid discoverability and reuse.

Overall, the article’s influence is best described as nascent but biologically pointed. Its immediate value lies in connecting mitochondrial depolarization to protein-level stabilization of a cytosolic B12 chaperone, a mechanism that may help explain how mitochondrial stress can reshape metabolic signaling. The current evidence base shows early scholarly reuse and broad indexing, but not yet the citation or public-discourse footprint that would support a stronger claim of established impact.
